# SK0232 — The argument or signature element is redundant

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

A trailing argument that restates the parameter's default, a delegate creation the conversion would have performed, lambda parameter types the target already declares, and an anonymous method's signature whose parameters nothing uses.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Cleanup |
| Default severity | warning |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, safe |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 2.0 |
| ReSharper | `RedundantArgumentDefaultValue` (`resharper_redundant_argument_default_value_highlighting`) |

## Why

An argument restating a default is a value that silently stops tracking the default the day it changes — the same hazard `optional-and-params-hazards` reports from the declaration side, seen from the call. `new EventHandler(Foo)` is an allocation as well as noise: the method group converts to the delegate on its own, and writing the conversion out produces exactly the same object through more text.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
Parse(text, throwOnFailure: false);
Process(text, 0);
changed += new EventHandler(OnChanged);
Func<int, int> twice = (int n) => n * 2;
EventHandler ignore = delegate(object? s, EventArgs e) { Log(); };
```

Write:

```csharp
Parse(text, throwOnFailure: false);
Process(text);
changed += OnChanged;
Func<int, int> twice = n => n * 2;
EventHandler ignore = delegate { Log(); };
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **Deleting an argument can change which method is called, and the rule asks the compiler rather than reasoning about it.** With `Foo(int a, int b = 0)` beside `Foo(int a)`, `Foo(1, 0)` and `Foo(1)` are calls to two different methods and nothing about the argument says so. Every finding re-binds the shortened call speculatively and withdraws unless the same symbol comes back, which is the guard Roslyn's own `IDE0004` family exists to remind everybody about. ⚠ **A call under a conditional access is refused outright, and the reason is a crash rather than a preference.** `store?.Read("name", true)` binds `.Read(…)` as a member *binding* whose receiver is the node above it, so the speculative rewrite — which has no parent — sends Roslyn's own `FindConditionalAccessNodeForBinding` off the top of the tree to dereference null. ⚠ **A caller-info parameter is excluded and looks exactly like the shape that is not.** Passing `null` to a `[CallerMemberName] string name = null` restates the default in the source and is the only thing keeping the value null: omit it and the compiler substitutes the caller's name. The same applies to `[CallerLineNumber]`, `[CallerFilePath]` and `[CallerArgumentExpression]`. ⚠ **The parameter a trailing argument fills is a fact only while the arguments do not outnumber the parameters.** An expanded `params` call has more arguments than parameters and no such pairing at all, so the scan is bounded on the *index* into the parameter list and never on the counter — bounding the counter is what threw `IndexOutOfRangeException` on every Serilog and every `string.Format` call for as long as the fixture harness did not assert on `AD0001` (#298). Positional arguments only — a named argument need not be last and need not fill the parameter its position names. A `params` parameter, a `ref`/`out`/`in` argument, and any argument whose value is not a compile-time constant equal to the default are all excluded; `default(SomeStruct)` is not a constant, so a struct default is never matched. ⚠ **Equal means equal in value across the numeric widenings**, so `Allow(name, 0)` against `long retries = 0` matches where a boxed `Equals` compared `int` against `long` and said no. `char` is deliberately outside that set: `Emit('A')` against `int code = 65` is the same number and not the same sentence. Consecutive trailing defaults are removed in **one** edit, longest suffix first, because one at a time would make the rule fire on its own output. ⚠ The three conversion shapes avoid overload resolution instead of answering it: each is reported only where the target type is written down — an explicitly typed variable or an assignment — because as an *argument* a method group, a lambda or an unsignatured `delegate` can be the thing that picks the overload. A method group only, never a delegate value (`new EventHandler(other)` is a copy) and never a lambda. Lambda parameter types are compared **including nullability**: `Func<string?, int> f = (string x) => x.Length;` compiles, and dropping the written type would introduce the `CS8602` the author wrote it to avoid. ⚠ **An anonymous method keeps its signature whenever the delegate declares an `out` parameter**, because a parameterless `delegate` is not convertible to such a type at all: the shortened form is `CS1688` rather than the same program. That shape exists only where the body throws, which is the one way an `out` parameter is legally never assigned. ⚠ **Three of the family's seven inspections are not covered**: `RedundantExplicitParamsArrayCreation` (`Foo(new object[] { arr })` and `Foo(arr)` pass the array in two different roles), `RedundantCallerArgumentExpressionDefaultValue`, which asks about a *declaration*'s unreachable default value rather than about a call, and `RedundantImmediateDelegateInvocation`, whose fix inlines a lambda body into an expression position and is a rewrite rather than a deletion. Constructor arguments and attribute arguments are not matched either; only invocations are.
